title: Literature reviews
examples: How do I know if I have found a research gap?
What is the difference between summarizing and synthesizing sources?
Should I just list what other people have said?

explain.say: Today we will learn about literature reviews for your studies. You need to know how to synthesize information effectively.
Synthesising means combining ideas from different sources. You are not just listing them separately. You are showing how they connect to each other.
Next we will focus on identifying recurring themes across your readings. Themes are the main ideas that keep appearing. They show patterns in the research.
Finally, we must pinpoint the research gap. This is what is missing from the current knowledge. It is the unanswered question your research will address.
For a real-life example, imagine studying climate change policy. You might find many sources on emissions reduction. But perhaps no one has looked at local community buy-in.
A common mistake is summarizing each article one by one. This just creates a report, not a review. You must actively group and compare the findings.

items: Show how ideas relate to each other.

faq.q: What is the difference between a summary and a synthesis?
faq.a: A summary just reports what one source says in its own words. Synthesis combines ideas from multiple sources to create a new understanding.
asks: Am I just retelling the articles?
Is synthesis just writing a conclusion?

faq.q: How do I know if there is a research gap?
faq.a: A gap exists when multiple sources discuss a topic but fail to address a specific angle. You look for what is consistently missing from the discussion.
asks: Does a gap mean I need more sources?
Is a gap always about geography?

faq.q: Should I use theory or empirical evidence in my review?
faq.a: You need both. Theories provide the framework, and empirical evidence provides the real-world data supporting or challenging those theories.
asks: Are theories and evidence separate things?
Do I need to use both types of sources?

faq.q: How long should my literature review be?
faq.a: The length depends on the assignment guidelines provided by your module leader. Always check the specific word count requirements.
asks: Does the length depend on the topic?

faq.q: What if I find conflicting evidence?
faq.a: Conflicting evidence is excellent for a review. You should discuss the conflict and suggest why the disagreement might exist.
asks: Is disagreement bad in academic writing?
How do I write about opposing views?

facts: Synthesis involves integrating multiple sources into a cohesive argument.
Themes represent recurring patterns or main ideas across various studies.
A research gap is an area where current knowledge is incomplete or contradictory.
A literature review must critically evaluate sources, not just describe them.

quiz.say: If Source X says A and Source Y says B, synthesis is best described as:
quiz.show: A. Listing A and B separately.

options.show: B. Only mentioning the most recent source.
options.say: B. Only mentioning the most recent source.

options.show: D. Summarizing A and then summarizing B.
options.say: D. Summarizing A and then summarizing B.

options.show: C. Explaining how A and B relate to each other.
options.say: C. Explaining how A and B relate to each other.

options.show: A. Stating that Source X is correct.
options.say: A. Stating that Source X is correct.

quiz.why: Synthesis requires you to build a connection between separate pieces of information.

wrong.0: This ignores the historical context provided by earlier research.
wrong.1: This is just summarizing, not synthesizing the connection.
wrong.3: This is biased and ignores the information from Source Y.

quiz.say: When identifying themes, you are looking for:

options.show: B. Ideas that keep appearing in different contexts.
options.say: B. Ideas that keep appearing in different contexts.

options.show: C. The single most important piece of data.
options.say: C. The single most important piece of data.

options.show: D. The conclusion of the last article read.
options.say: D. The conclusion of the last article read.

quiz.why: Themes are the recurring conceptual threads that run through your literature.

wrong.1: Controversy is interesting, but a theme is a broader pattern.
wrong.2: Focusing on one data point misses the broader conceptual pattern.
wrong.3: Your review must synthesize, not just report the last thing you read.

quiz.say: Your research gap is best identified when:

options.show: C. You find three sources that contradict each other.
options.say: C. You find three sources that contradict each other.

options.show: D. You read sources from only one country.
options.say: D. You read sources from only one country.

options.show: A. Multiple sources discuss a topic but ignore one aspect.
options.say: A. Multiple sources discuss a topic but ignore one aspect.

options.show: B. You disagree with every source you read.
options.say: B. You disagree with every source you read.

quiz.why: The gap is the specific niche that existing research has overlooked or not fully explored.

wrong.0: Contradiction is a type of gap, but a gap can also be about lack of scope.
wrong.1: A gap can exist even if sources are plentiful, if they are all geographically limited.
wrong.3: Disagreement is fine, but a gap is about what is missing, not just what is wrong.
